articles.title: ‘Will letters save poor patients’ lives?’ BJP exposes procurement failures under Karnataka Congress govt
articles.description: BENGALURU: The BJP has accused the Karnataka government of failing to clear outstanding payments to pharmaceutical companies, alleging that mounting dues and delays in tender procedures have discouraged suppliers from participating in government procurement and affected the availability of essential medicines and medical equipment in state-run hospitals. Leader of the Opposition in the Assembly R. Ashoka said that pharmaceutical companies were reluctant to supply medicines to government hospitals because the state had not settled payments for earlier supplies. He claimed that even established companies were avoiding tenders due to uncertainty over when their bills would be cleared. In a statement, Ashoka accused the Congress government of creating a situation in which poor patients were bearing the consequences of administrative and financial failures. He described the alleged disruption as the result of what he called the government’s “guarantee politics”, claiming that implementing welfare guarantees had left the state treasury under pressure and led to mounting unpaid bills. Ashoka alleged that suppliers who had provided medicines and equipment to government institutions were being forced to wait for payments, affecting their ability and willingness to participate in subsequent procurement processes. According to him, the loss of confidence among pharmaceutical companies could further complicate the supply of life-saving medicines to government hospitals. ದಿವಾಳಿ ಸರ್ಕಾರದ ಬಾಕಿಗೆ ಹೆದರಿ ಯಾವ ಔಷಧ ಕಂಪನಿಗಳು ಸರಬರಾಜು ಮಾಡಲು ಮುಂದೆ ಬರುತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ! ಇದು ಪಾಪರ್ ಕಾಂಗ್ರೆಸ್ ಸರ್ಕಾರದ ಗ್ಯಾರೆಂಟಿ ಎಫೆಕ್ಟ್! ಸರ್ಕಾರಿ ಆಸ್ಪತ್ರೆಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಬಡ ರೋಗಿಗಳಿಗೆ ಜೀವರಕ್ಷಕ ಔಷಧಗಳು ಮತ್ತು ಉಪಕರಣಗಳು ಸಿಗದ ಪರಿಸ್ಥಿತಿ ನಿರ್ಮಾಣವಾಗಿದೆ. ಪೂರೈಸಿದ ಔಷಧಗಳ ಬಿಲ್‌ಗಳಿಗೆ ಸಕಾಲದಲ್ಲಿ ಹಣ ಬಿಡುಗಡೆ ಮಾಡದೆ… pic.twitter.com/3wTXDccAc7 — R. Ashoka (@RAshokaBJP) November 23, 2026 He also questioned the functioning of the Karnataka State Medical Supplies Corporation Limited (KSMSCL), the nodal agency responsible for procuring drugs, consumables and medical equipment for healthcare institutions under the state Health and Family Welfare Department. The BJP leader alleged that the corporation had become dysfunctional due to commission-related activities, delays in processing tenders, official negligence, and administrative shortcomings. He claimed that these problems had weakened the procurement system and affected the timely availability of essential medical supplies. Ashoka further pointed to a letter from Health Minister U.T. Khader to the corporation’s commissioner, in which the minister reportedly highlighted several shortcomings in its functioning. He argued that the minister’s communication itself reflected the seriousness of the problems within the department. Questioning the government’s response, Ashoka asked whether writing letters and seeking reports from officials would address the difficulties faced by patients dependent on public healthcare facilities. He maintained that the government needed to move beyond correspondence and take immediate administrative and financial decisions to restore suppliers’ confidence. “Will merely writing letters and calling for reports save poor patients’ lives?” he asked, while accusing the government of failing to address the problems affecting medicine procurement and distribution. The BJP leader directly targeted Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar, demanding that the government clear pending bills without further delay and ensure that hospitals receive the medicines and equipment required for patient care. He urged the Chief Minister to intervene immediately and hold the officials concerned accountable for the lapses. The controversy comes amid fresh allegations of irregularities in KSMSCL’s functioning. A Bengaluru-based lawyer, A.C. Vishnuprasad, recently submitted a complaint to the Governor, Chief Minister and Chief Secretary seeking a high-level inquiry into alleged tender irregularities, kickbacks and corruption in the corporation. In his complaint dated November 17, the lawyer alleged that commissions were being collected from companies, confidential tender information was being leaked, and certain suppliers were being favoured. He also sought an examination of allegations that ministerial relatives had influenced tender processes. The complaint referred to the Health Minister’s letter highlighting operational shortcomings and called for scrutiny of technical qualifications, work orders, supply records, quality checks and payment clearances. The complaint has, however, brought additional attention to the procurement and administrative issues surrounding the corporation. KSMSCL was established in October 2020 and functions as the state’s central agency for procuring medicines, consumables and equipment for government healthcare institutions. Its role is crucial because timely procurement and distribution are essential for maintaining stocks at government hospitals and other public health facilities. Also Read: Keralam: Dhanaraj Murder verdict setback to CPM as Court rejects RSS conspiracy charge The corporation’s official website continues to list drug and equipment tenders, including procurement notices issued for the 2026-27 financial year. However, the BJP’s central allegation is that delays in clearing suppliers’ dues and shortcomings in tender administration are discouraging companies from participating in the procurement process. Ashoka said the government must recognise that supply-chain interruptions could directly affect patients who cannot afford to buy medicines from private pharmacies. He demanded immediate clearance of outstanding payments, corrective action against officials responsible for administrative lapses and measures to ensure uninterrupted supplies to hospitals.

articles.title: Modi–Balen Shah Meeting: A New Era of India–Nepal Economic Relations and Opportunities for Indian MSMEs
articles.description: Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah, popularly known as Balen Shah, concluded his two-day state visit to India on November 23, 2026, following extensive bilateral discussions with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The visit, which took place on November 22–23, marks a significant milestone in the evolving relationship between the two neighbouring countries. For both New Delhi and Kathmandu, the engagement represents much more than a conventional diplomatic exercise. It comes at a time when Nepal is undergoing a significant political and generational transformation, India is strengthening its regional economic leadership, and South Asia is witnessing an increasingly competitive geopolitical environment. The two leaders adopted a joint vision titled “Viksit Bharat and Samunnat Nepal”, establishing a comprehensive framework for cooperation in trade, investment, infrastructure, energy, technology, entrepreneurship, education and climate resilience. India also announced a ₹15,000-crore development cooperation package for Nepal, alongside several infrastructure initiatives and eight memorandums of understanding covering diverse areas of bilateral cooperation. From SMEStreet’s economic perspective, the most significant dimension of this engagement is its potential to transform India–Nepal relations from a largely conventional trading partnership into an interconnected regional economic ecosystem, creating opportunities for manufacturers, technology companies, exporters, startups and micro, small and medium enterprises on both sides of the border. Key Highlights of Balen Shah’s India Visit India announced a ₹15,000-crore development cooperation package for Nepal. ₹11,500 crore has been earmarked as a line of credit for energy sector projects. ₹3,500 crore will be provided as grant assistance for reconstruction and infrastructure. India–Nepal bilateral merchandise trade reached approximately $9.39 billion in FY 2025–26. Foundation stone laid for the 669 MW Lower Arun Hydroelectric Project. Cross-border special economic zones and industrial parks proposed. Agro-industrial park announced in Chitwan, Nepal. Enhanced access to Indian seaports for Nepalese transit trade. Expanded cooperation in artificial intelligence, digital payments and startups. Eight memorandums of understanding signed. Why Balen Shah’s India Visit Is Strategically Important The emergence of Balendra Shah as Nepal’s prime minister represents a significant departure from the country's traditional political establishment. A former mayor of Kathmandu, structural engineer and rapper, Shah represents a younger generation of political leadership that has built its appeal around governance, accountability, infrastructure development and economic aspirations. For India, engagement with this emerging political leadership provides an opportunity to establish a relationship that extends beyond conventional government-to-government diplomacy. Nepal’s younger generation is increasingly concerned with employment generation, entrepreneurship, technology adoption, urban infrastructure and reducing the economic necessity of migration overseas. India, with its expanding digital economy, manufacturing capabilities and startup ecosystem, can potentially become an important partner in addressing these aspirations. Shah’s visit to New Delhi also underscores India’s continuing importance in Kathmandu’s foreign policy calculations, despite Nepal’s efforts to diversify its international economic partnerships. The visit carries considerable humanitarian and economic significance following the devastating floods that affected Nepal in August 2026. India’s newly announced financial assistance is intended to support reconstruction and long-term development. If implemented effectively, the assistance could stimulate domestic demand in Nepal, support employment, encourage private investment and generate new requirements for industrial equipment, engineering services, construction materials and technology. For India, supporting Nepal’s economic stability is also a matter of regional economic interest. A prosperous and stable Nepal offers greater opportunities for trade, cross-border investment and sustainable development across India’s northern and eastern states. Narendra Modi and Balen Shah: A New Diplomatic Equation The relationship between Narendra Modi and Balendra Shah presents an interesting combination of political experience and generational change. While Modi represents an established model of national leadership focused on infrastructure development, economic expansion, digital transformation and international engagement, Shah represents a younger political leadership emerging from urban governance and public demands for administrative accountability. Despite their different political journeys, there are several areas of convergence between their respective development agendas. The official joint vision reflects shared priorities in infrastructure-led economic development, technology-enabled governance, entrepreneurship promotion, employment generation, renewable energy and regional connectivity. The inclusion of good governance, digital public infrastructure and civil service capacity building in the bilateral framework is particularly noteworthy. Shah’s background in municipal governance and Modi’s emphasis on technology-driven public administration could provide common ground for institutional cooperation. The relationship also has the potential to move beyond conventional diplomatic engagements dominated by political and security considerations towards economic performance and measurable developmental outcomes. However, it would be premature to conclude that the two leaders have established a particularly close personal relationship after one summit. Their diplomatic compatibility will ultimately be tested by the ability of their respective administrations to implement agreements, address longstanding disagreements and deliver tangible economic benefits. India’s Neighbourhood First Policy and the China Factor Balen Shah’s engagement with India should not necessarily be interpreted as Nepal distancing itself from China. Kathmandu has considerable economic interests in maintaining productive relationships with both its larger neighbours. Nepal’s geographical location gives it the potential to become an important economic bridge between the two major Asian economies. India enjoys geographical, cultural and commercial advantages that are difficult to replicate. The open border, historical family connections, established supply chains, access to Indian ports and a shared economic history provide the foundation for a distinctive bilateral partnership. However, these advantages cannot be taken for granted. Nepal has its own legitimate aspirations for economic independence, strategic autonomy and diversified international engagement. India’s competitive advantage lies in offering commercially viable infrastructure, affordable technology, access to a large consumer market and dependable economic connectivity. For Narendra Modi, cultivating a constructive relationship with Balen Shah could strengthen India’s regional influence without requiring Nepal to compromise its strategic autonomy. The most sustainable approach would be to make economic cooperation with India sufficiently attractive that Nepalese businesses, investors and consumers naturally benefit from deeper engagement. Understanding India’s ₹15,000-Crore Development Package for Nepal One of the most consequential announcements of Balen Shah’s visit was India’s development cooperation package worth ₹15,000 crore, equivalent to NPR 24,000 crore. According to the official joint statement issued on November 23, 2026, the financial assistance comprises ₹3,500 crore in grants for post-disaster reconstruction and new infrastructure projects, alongside a rupee-denominated line of credit worth ₹11,500 crore for energy sector projects. The composition of the package is particularly important from an economic perspective. Nearly 77 per cent of the assistance has been allocated towards energy financing, while approximately 23 per cent will support reconstruction and infrastructure development through grants. The entire package should therefore not be interpreted as an unconditional grant or immediate government expenditure. Specific projects, financing arrangements, procurement conditions and implementation schedules will be determined through bilateral consultations. From an Indian industry perspective, the package could eventually generate considerable demand for electrical machinery, power transmission equipment, engineering services, construction materials, industrial pumps, transformers, cables, water management solutions, disaster mitigation technologies and project management services. While large engineering and infrastructure companies may emerge as principal contractors, a significant portion of the industrial supply chain could involve specialised Indian MSMEs. India–Nepal Economic Relations: A $9.39-Billion Trade Partnership India continues to be Nepal’s largest trading partner and its largest source of foreign investment. Geographical proximity, established distribution networks and transit arrangements give Indian enterprises a considerable commercial advantage. According to data published by the Indian Embassy in Kathmandu, bilateral merchandise trade reached approximately $9.39 billion during FY 2025–26. India accounted for approximately 62.3 per cent of Nepal’s overall merchandise trade, while Nepal emerged as India’s 12th-largest export destination during the financial year. Indian exports to Nepal primarily include petroleum products, iron and steel, automobiles, machinery and agricultural commodities. Nepalese exports to India include edible oils, cardamom, iron products, plywood, jute and processed agricultural products. India–Nepal Bilateral Trade Performance FY 2021–22: $11.02 billion FY 2022–23: $8.92 billion FY 2023–24: $7.87 billion FY 2024–25: $8.67 billion FY 2025–26: $9.39 billion During FY 2025–26, Indian merchandise exports to Nepal stood at approximately $7.45 billion, while Nepalese exports to India reached approximately $1.94 billion. The bilateral trade data reveals an interesting economic trend. Although overall trade remains below its FY 2021–22 peak, it has recovered substantially from the FY 2023–24 levels. Between FY 2024–25 and FY 2025–26, bilateral merchandise trade increased by approximately 8.2 per cent. Indian exports to Nepal grew by approximately 0.8 per cent, while Nepalese exports to India increased by nearly 51 per cent. This changing trade composition could be beneficial for the long-term sustainability of bilateral economic relations. A stronger Nepalese export economy would improve domestic purchasing capacity, support industrialisation and potentially create additional demand for Indian machinery, technology, intermediate goods and professional services. India must therefore look at Nepal not merely as an export market but also as a prospective manufacturing and value-chain partner. Hydropower Could Become the Backbone of India–Nepal Economic Cooperation Nepal’s hydropower resources represent one of its most valuable long-term economic assets. India’s expanding electricity market, meanwhile, offers Nepal a commercially significant export destination for renewable energy. During Balen Shah’s visit, the two prime ministers laid the foundation stone for the 669 MW Lower Arun Hydroelectric Project, providing further momentum to bilateral energy cooperation. This development complements the existing 900 MW Arun-III project and the long-term power trade agreement signed in 2024, which envisages exports of up to 10,000 MW of electricity from Nepal to India over a decade. The newly announced ₹11,500-crore energy sector line of credit further strengthens the foundation for bilateral collaboration. For Indian MSMEs, this emerging energy corridor could create opportunities extending beyond conventional power equipment manufacturing. Enterprises specialising in industrial automation, power electronics, switchgear, electrical panels, cables, transformers, sensors, predictive maintenance, turbine components and water monitoring systems could find new markets. Indian technology startups working in renewable energy management, smart grids, environmental monitoring and energy efficiency could also benefit from the expansion of Nepal’s energy infrastructure. Nepal’s hydropower development could generate recurring opportunities for maintenance, equipment replacement, technical consulting and industrial services over several decades. However, financing, environmental approvals, transmission capacity, seasonal variations in electricity generation and project execution remain important challenges. Cross-Border Industrial Zones: A Game Changer for Indian MSMEs Perhaps the most important announcement from an MSME perspective is the proposal to develop cross-border special economic zones and industrial parks near the India–Nepal border. The joint vision recognises the potential to integrate manufacturing and processing supply chains across the two countries. If implemented effectively, this initiative could introduce an entirely new dimension to regional industrialisation. Indian MSMEs could supply machinery, components, raw materials, industrial designs, technology and manufacturing expertise to Nepalese industrial units. Nepalese enterprises could participate in agricultural processing, packaging, assembly and other value-added activities, with finished products potentially accessing domestic and international markets, subject to applicable trade regulations. Such a model could particularly benefit industrial clusters in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Uttarakhand, West Bengal and Delhi-NCR. Manufacturers from Gujarat, Maharashtra, Punjab, Haryana and other industrial states could also explore commercial partnerships with Nepalese businesses. Cross-border industrial collaboration could provide Indian MSMEs with opportunities to expand their international presence without immediately establishing expensive manufacturing operations in distant markets. However, the success of these industrial zones will depend on predictable taxation, customs arrangements, rules of origin, electricity availability, logistics infrastructure, labour regulations and investment protection. Chitwan Agro-Industrial Park: Opportunities for Food Processing MSMEs The proposed establishment of an agro-industrial park in Chitwan, with Indian grant assistance, deserves special attention. Nepal has considerable agricultural potential, but inadequate processing facilities, fragmented supply chains and limited storage infrastructure constrain value addition. Indian MSMEs have developed extensive capabilities in affordable agricultural machinery, food processing equipment, packaging technology, refrigeration and cold-chain solutions. The proposed industrial park could create opportunities for Indian businesses operating in fruit and vegetable processing, dairy technology, grain milling, food dehydration, agricultural equipment, irrigation and sustainable packaging. There is also scope for joint development of organic food products, herbal products, spices, tea and other agricultural commodities. Rather than merely exporting finished food products to Nepal, Indian companies could establish partnerships that support Nepalese producers in improving productivity, processing capabilities and market access. Such collaborations could help build a more balanced bilateral trade relationship while creating recurring demand for Indian industrial technology. Digital Economy, Artificial Intelligence and Startups: The Next Frontier The Modi–Balen Shah engagement has placed technology and innovation among the central pillars of bilateral cooperation. The joint vision includes plans for a startup centre in Kathmandu, an innovation hub in Pokhara, digital parks, data centres, artificial intelligence collaboration and expanded cooperation in digital governance. There is also an emphasis on developing AI capabilities for the Nepali language through collaboration involving India’s Bhashini initiative. For India’s technology MSMEs and startups, Nepal offers an opportunity to enter a geographically accessible international market. India’s experience in building affordable and scalable digital solutions could be particularly relevant to Nepal, where businesses may require cost-effective alternatives to expensive global enterprise software. Indian companies specialising in enterprise resource planning, accounting software, fintech, cybersecurity, healthcare technology, educational platforms, artificial intelligence and cloud-based business solutions could explore opportunities in Nepal. Small technology companies could also collaborate with Nepalese startups to jointly develop localised software products. The expansion of digital payments could further reduce friction for tourism operators, retailers and service providers. India’s Unified Payments Interface and Nepal’s national payment infrastructure already have linkages. The latest bilateral framework seeks to advance retail payment interoperability. However, retail payment connectivity should not be confused with unrestricted cross-border commercial settlements. Business transactions must comply with applicable foreign exchange, banking and regulatory requirements. Improved Connectivity Could Reduce the Cost of Doing Business For decades, physical connectivity has remained central to India–Nepal economic relations. Nepal’s landlocked geography makes efficient access to Indian transport networks and seaports particularly important. The November 2026 engagement provides additional momentum to railway infrastructure, petroleum pipelines, road bridges and integrated border check posts. Additional port access through Deendayal Port in Kandla, Gujarat, and prospective access to Paradip Port in Odisha could diversify Nepal’s international trade routes. Similarly, the proposed Raxaul–Kathmandu railway could eventually transform freight and passenger movement if it progresses from planning to construction and operation. For MSMEs, improved connectivity has implications beyond transportation costs. It could reduce inventory requirements, delivery uncertainties, product damage and working capital tied up in goods awaiting customs clearance. Smaller enterprises could benefit disproportionately from these improvements because they typically have less financial capacity to absorb logistics delays than larger corporations. The expansion of connectivity could also create opportunities for logistics companies, warehousing operators, freight technology startups, packaging manufacturers and transportation service providers. Healthcare, Pharmaceuticals and Medical Technology Healthcare represents another significant area of emerging India–Nepal economic cooperation. The bilateral vision includes strengthening healthcare infrastructure, improving access to affordable medicines, upgrading Nepal’s medical laboratory capabilities and promoting institutional collaboration. Indian pharmaceutical MSMEs, medical equipment manufacturers, diagnostic companies, hospital management software providers and telemedicine startups could explore opportunities in Nepal. India’s ability to provide affordable generic medicines and cost-effective healthcare technology could complement Nepal’s efforts to expand access to quality healthcare. There is also potential for collaboration in Ayurveda, traditional medicine, wellness products and preventive healthcare. However, companies entering these segments must comply with Nepalese drug registration requirements, medical device regulations and applicable product quality standards. Religious Tourism as an MSME Growth Engine The launch of the Sarayu–Kamala Express between Ayodhya and Janakpur represents the commercial potential of India and Nepal’s shared cultural heritage. The two countries have also identified opportunities to develop Buddhist and Shiva–Shakti tourism circuits. These initiatives could generate commercial opportunities for hotels, homestays, restaurants, travel agencies, handicraft manufacturers, traditional garment businesses, tour operators and digital travel platforms. Religious tourism is particularly relevant to micro and small enterprises because a substantial portion of visitor expenditure reaches local service providers. Artisans in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and other Indian states could benefit from increased demand for traditional products, souvenirs and devotional merchandise. Joint tourism packages covering Ayodhya, Janakpur, Varanasi, Pashupatinath, Bodh Gaya and Lumbini could create an interconnected regional tourism economy. This could also encourage collaboration between Indian and Nepalese entrepreneurs in experiential tourism, wellness tourism, adventure tourism and hospitality management. Ten Indian MSME Sectors That Could Benefit From Balen Shah’s India Visit 1. Electrical Equipment and Renewable Energy: Demand for transformers, switchgear, cables, control panels, industrial automation and hydropower components. 2. Engineering and Construction: Opportunities in infrastructure projects, construction machinery, prefabricated structures and engineering services. 3. Agriculture and Food Processing: Demand for agricultural equipment, food processing machinery, cold-chain solutions and packaging technology. 4. Information Technology and Artificial Intelligence: Opportunities in SaaS, ERP, cybersecurity, local-language AI and enterprise digitisation. 5. Logistics and Warehousing: Growth potential in cross-border transportation, freight management, storage facilities and supply-chain technology. 6. Healthcare and Pharmaceuticals: Opportunities in affordable medicines, medical equipment, diagnostic services and digital healthcare platforms. 7. Tourism and Hospitality: Expansion of religious tourism, travel services, hotels, homestays and cultural tourism. 8. Textiles and Handicrafts: Cross-border sourcing, distribution, traditional products and value-added manufacturing. 9. Education and Skill Development: Opportunities for vocational training, entrepreneurship development, professional certification and educational technology. 10. Consumer Goods: Expansion of distribution networks for affordable Indian products across Nepalese markets. The largest immediate opportunities are likely to emerge in reconstruction, engineering, industrial equipment and infrastructure-related supply chains, subject to project approvals and procurement timelines. Technology, agro-processing, healthcare and professional services could represent more scalable medium-term opportunities. Can India–Nepal Bilateral Trade Reach $15 Billion by 2030? The current bilateral merchandise trade base of approximately $9.39 billion provides considerable room for expansion. Infrastructure development, industrial cooperation, rising Nepalese purchasing capacity and improved trade facilitation could collectively accelerate bilateral commerce over the next four financial years. SMEStreet’s indicative economic projections present three possible scenarios. Conservative Scenario: At an annual compound growth rate of 5 per cent, bilateral merchandise trade could reach approximately $11.41 billion by FY 2029–30. Base Case Scenario: At an annual compound growth rate of 9 per cent, bilateral merchandise trade could reach approximately $13.25 billion. Optimistic Scenario: At an annual compound growth rate of 13 per cent, bilateral merchandise trade could reach approximately $15.31 billion. These projections are illustrative and do not represent official government forecasts. Under the optimistic scenario, India–Nepal merchandise trade could cross $15 billion by the end of the decade. However, achieving this level would require sustained double-digit growth, faster project execution, greater private sector participation and meaningful improvements in cross-border logistics. The emerging opportunities in services, technology and energy cooperation could add another dimension to the economic relationship, although their contributions must be assessed separately. Challenges Before Narendra Modi and Balen Shah Despite the positive atmosphere surrounding the visit, several structural challenges remain. The disagreements concerning Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura remain important political issues. While the two countries have committed to resolving outstanding matters through bilateral dialogue, the territorial disagreements have not been settled. The joint vision also allows for the review of existing bilateral agreements, including the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, through mutual consent. Another important challenge is Nepal’s substantial merchandise trade deficit with India. New Delhi should encourage Nepalese exports, manufacturing investments and industrial capacity building to establish a more mutually beneficial commercial relationship. Project implementation is equally important. Land acquisition, environmental approvals, financing arrangements and bureaucratic coordination can delay infrastructure development. A delayed industrial park or transmission project provides little immediate commercial benefit to MSMEs. Access to public procurement is another significant concern. Large infrastructure contracts tend to favour established corporations with substantial financial and technical capabilities. Without transparent procurement mechanisms, vendor development programmes and accessible subcontracting arrangements, smaller Indian and Nepalese enterprises may struggle to participate. Indian MSMEs must also carefully evaluate payment security, customs procedures, product certifications, tax implications and the credibility of local distribution partners. What Indian MSMEs Should Do Now Indian industry associations, export promotion councils and MSME entrepreneurs should begin preparing for emerging commercial opportunities rather than waiting for all infrastructure projects to become operational. Indian manufacturers should identify sector-specific demand in Nepal and establish relationships with local distributors, industrial associations and prospective buyers. Businesses specialising in infrastructure equipment should monitor procurement announcements, project development schedules and vendor registration opportunities. Technology companies should explore partnerships with Nepalese startups and enterprises to develop affordable, localised digital solutions. Indian exporters should also evaluate opportunities to establish local distribution, service centres, assembly facilities and joint ventures. Institutions such as the Federation of Indian Export Organisations, Engineering Export Promotion Council, EXIM Bank of India, Indian Embassy in Kathmandu and Federation of Nepalese Chambers of Commerce and Industry could serve as important facilitators. Entrepreneurs should verify project eligibility and procurement requirements before making significant financial commitments. SMEStreet’s Perspective: The Need for an India–Nepal MSME Economic Corridor The Modi–Balen Shah diplomatic engagement provides an appropriate foundation for establishing a dedicated India–Nepal MSME Economic Corridor. Such an initiative could provide institutional support for entrepreneurs seeking cross-border business opportunities and ensure that the benefits of high-level diplomatic engagement reach smaller enterprises. SMEStreet recommends that policymakers, industry associations and business leaders explore the following initiatives: Establishment of an India–Nepal MSME Business Council. Annual bilateral MSME and startup summits. Sector-specific buyer-seller meetings. Cross-border entrepreneurship development programmes. Vendor development initiatives for infrastructure projects. Export facilitation centres in Indian border states. A digital marketplace for verified Indian and Nepalese business partners. Joint venture and technology transfer facilitation. Export finance, credit insurance and payment support. Bilateral commercial grievance redressal mechanisms. A structured industry engagement mechanism could significantly improve awareness, market access and business confidence among MSMEs. The proposed economic corridor should not merely focus on increasing Indian exports. It should also encourage Nepalese entrepreneurship, local manufacturing, technology transfer and mutually beneficial industrial partnerships. Conclusion: From Political Diplomacy to Entrepreneurial Diplomacy Balendra Shah’s state visit to India represents a potentially important turning point in India–Nepal relations. The combination of infrastructure financing, energy cooperation, industrial development, digital innovation and cultural connectivity creates an opportunity for both nations to build a more sophisticated and mutually beneficial economic partnership. For Narendra Modi, the engagement provides an opportunity to reinforce India’s regional development leadership. For Balen Shah, it offers access to financial resources, industrial expertise, technology and a substantial neighbouring market. For Indian MSMEs, the visit could open new international business opportunities across manufacturing, renewable energy, food processing, healthcare, technology, logistics and tourism. However, the real success of this partnership will not be measured merely by the number of agreements signed or the size of financial assistance announced. It will be measured by the number of businesses created, jobs generated, infrastructure projects completed, entrepreneurs empowered and cross-border commercial partnerships established. The next chapter of India–Nepal relations should not be written by political leaders alone. It should also be written by entrepreneurs, innovators, manufacturers and the MSMEs of both countries. If New Delhi and Kathmandu can translate their shared political vision into a practical framework for entrepreneurial collaboration, the Modi–Balen Shah engagement could eventually emerge as an important milestone in South Asia’s regional economic integration. Source: Prime Minister’s Office, Government of India; Press Information Bureau; Indian Embassy in Kathmandu; Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India. Future trade projections and business opportunity assessments are indicative and do not constitute official government forecasts or guaranteed commercial outcomes.

articles.title: FPJ Exclusive: How Indian AI Startup Zelmier Is Cutting Government Tender Preparation Time From Hours To Under 10 Minutes
articles.description: In an exclusive interview with FPJ Tech Editor Tasneem Kanchwala, Zelmier founder Pranjal Srivastava reveals how his AI startup is reducing government tender discovery and bid preparation time to eight to nine minutes. The bootstrapped startup tracks 82 government platforms and serves 144 businesses.
